title: Reading your energy bill without the headache
description: A bill becomes much less mysterious once you know which three numbers actually matter.

body.heading: Find the three numbers that matter
paragraphs: Most energy bills are crowded with codes and tables, but three figures explain almost everything: how much energy you used, measured in kilowatt-hours (kWh); the price you pay for each unit; and any fixed daily or monthly standing charge that applies whatever you use.

Multiply the units used by the unit price, add the standing charge for the period, and you should land close to the total. If your estimate is wildly different, something on the bill is worth a phone call.

body.heading: Actual readings versus estimates
paragraphs: Bills based on estimated readings can drift away from reality for months. If your bill says estimated, compare the number with your actual meter. A quick photo of the meter gives you a dated record to refer back to.
Sending a real reading, or letting a smart meter do it for you, smooths out surprises. It also means a sudden jump on the bill points to a real change at home rather than a paperwork catch-up.

body.heading: What the bill can teach you
paragraphs: Compare this bill with the same season last year rather than with last month. Heating and lighting swing so much with the seasons that month-to-month comparisons mislead.

If usage has crept up year on year, think about what changed: a new appliance, more people at home, or longer heating hours. The bill cannot tell you which device is responsible, but it can tell you whether your small saving habits are adding up.

takeaway: Check the units used, the unit price and the standing charge, and your bill will mostly explain itself.
